question: Have specialized approaches been developed for providing LLM assistance when people author SQL queries?

sections.title: Distinct Challenges of SQL Authoring
sections.text: SQL presents three main challenges that warrant special treatment rather than casting it as just another programming language for existing LLM autocompletion systems [1]. A primary difficulty is that coexisting with the traditional auto complete system is a challenge faced by many AI-assisted code authoring solutions [1]. Furthermore, the latency constraints are much tighter for an autocompletion tool compared to natural language querying [1]. This issue is pronounced in LLM-based text-to-SQL systems, where generating SQL queries is slower than traditional language modeling, posing a challenge for developing efficient, localized NL interfaces to databases (NLIDB) [2]. Additionally, for automixting SQL queries, the LLM must be trained on a large number of SQL queries instead of text-sql pairs [1].

sections.title: Architectural Innovations for Efficiency
sections.text: To address latency issues, Consistency large language models (CLLMs) have been developed with an enhanced model architecture, providing a solution to reduce latency and speed up SQL query generation [2]. RAG-based text-to-SQL systems also integrate dynamic retrieval abilities with generative models to improve SQL query generation [2]. For schema management, SchemaGraphSQL offers efficient schema linking using pathfinding graph algorithms for text-to-sql on large-scale databases [5]. Another approach involves scaling Text2SQL via LLM-efficient Schema Filtering with Functional Dependency Graph Rerankers [4]. BiomedSQL has been developed for text-to-SQL for scientific reasoning on biomedical knowledge bases [4]. Prompting techniques like Chain-of-Thought (Wei et al., 2022) and ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) have demonstrated improved performance on multi-step reasoning tasks in both general and biomedical settings [3].

sections.text: SQLCompose helps developers bootstrap and iterate on complex SQL queries without needing to navigate clunky SQL syntax, semantics, or documentation, with the biggest time savings coming from iterative development [1]. To handle non-sequential SQL writing, SQLComposeFIM is a fill-in-the-middle model developed to have context before and after the line(s) of code to be completed [1]. This design helps the model consume context bidirectionally, utilizing code before and code after [1]. The LCM component overcomes the limitations imposed by regular CM objective with respect to tokenization [1]. Infilling models were trained following the concept of causal masking, where parts of a training sequence are moved to the end, and the reordered sequence is predicted autoregressively [1]. Pre-training on first-party SQL queries and schema equips the model with knowledge of the first-party data warehouse, which is very important to prevent the model from hallucinating table and column names while synthesizing SQL queries [1]. question: How are user demonstrations represented in domain-specific-language programs and used for automation tasks?

sections.title: Representation of Demonstrations in DSLs
sections.text: Domain-specific languages for automation represent user demonstrations through distinct structural abstractions. In the Pumice system, an end-user programmable agent, procedural actions are encoded as sequences of GUI operations, while declarative concepts are defined by references to GUI contents [2][2][2]. These concepts are further formalized as typed resolve() functions within the parsing result, indicating they require subsequent resolution [2]. Pumice identifies and learns three specific types of unknown components from user utterances: procedures, Boolean concepts, and value concepts [2]. This representation addresses the challenge that end users often employ unclear, ambiguous, or vague concepts when instructing tasks in natural language, particularly when specifying conditionals [2]. In contrast, DiLogics employs program synthesis techniques to record user actions and their symbolic relationships within the web DOM structure [1]. By recording mappings between diverse specifications and UI actions, DiLogics constructs automation programs with malleable programming logic, inserting proper UI actions for each step in real time to fulfill diverse task specifications.

In addition, DiLogics employs program synthesis techniques to record the user’s actions and their symbolic relationships in the web DOM structure.

Pumice can detect and learn three kinds of unknown components in user utterances: procedures , Boolean concepts , and value concepts .
Both kinds of concepts are represented as typed resolve() functions in the parsing result (shown in Figure 1 ), indicating that they need to be further resolved down the line.

To support programming for tasks in diverse domains, we leverage the graphical user interfaces (GUIs) of existing third-party mobile apps as a medium, where procedural actions are represented as sequences of GUI operations, and declarative concepts can be represented through references to GUI contents.
Existing systems have limited support for letting the user teach agents new concepts or explaining unclear concepts.

In this paper, we address the research challenge of enabling end users to augment domain-independent task automation scripts with conditional structures and new concepts through a combination of natural language programming and programming by demonstration (PBD).

sections.title: Demonstration Capture and Pattern Detection
sections.text: The process of capturing demonstrations is designed to reduce the expertise required from non-expert users, allowing them to interact with target applications rather than writing code [1]. In DiLogics, users initiate web recording and demonstrate actions for each task step from the start of the task. The system semantically segments input data to decompose the task into more tractable steps [1]. As users demonstrate actions, the system detects repetitive patterns; for instance, after demonstrating for two iterations (i.e. two rows), DiLogics detects the repetitive pattern in the user action trace and generates an automation program. Following this detection, the system enters a semi-automation stage for the third iteration, where it prompts users with the predicted action. Every web macro is recorded and used to synthesize a repeatable program, such as a for-loop. This synthesis is enabled by a program synthesis engine based on WebRobot, which performs inferences based on input data and website structures.

sections.title: Generalization and Execution Logic
sections.text: To apply recorded demonstrations to new tasks, systems utilize semantic matching and generalization. DiLogics constructs a catalog of step-to-UI action mappings. During later automation, the system inspects this catalog to find the most similar demonstrated step via semantic matching. It then generalizes the stored UI action sequence to the current step and automates based on the current highlighted content. By constantly searching for and locating the most semantically similar element, the automation can execute macros on the correct UI regardless of website DOM structure, going beyond structural inferences and layout constraints. DiLogics extends WebRobot's functionality by incorporating semantic search in its automation execution. This approach allows web macros to be generalized to semantically similar tasks. However, a limitation of this PBD system using NLP for web automation is that it cannot perform logics requiring constant website state analysis. Pumice similarly allows users to augment domain-independent scripts with conditional structures and new concepts via natural language and PBD [2], addressing the limited support in existing systems for letting users teach agents new concepts or explaining unclear concepts [2].

question: How can I use an hybridization of ontology and machine learning for text summarization ?

sections.title: System Architecture and Ontology Design
sections.text: The OATS system integrates ontology and machine learning into two primary modules: ontology-based topic identification and user-focused text summarization [1]. It employs a simplified COVID-19 Risk Factor ontology, derived from a novel CQM ontology, which excludes the "Change Concept" and defines a "Population" consisting of two "Health Statuses": a specific risk factor and COVID-19 [1]. This ontology utilizes concept graphs to represent knowledge extracted from unstructured text [2] [1]. To construct these graphs, the system uses the igraph package in the R programming language to create graph concepts from extracted triples [1]. This approach allows the system to extract summary sentences from unstructured text without relying on manually annotated knowledge, distinguishing it from other ontology-based automatic text summarization (ATS) systems [1].

sections.title: Machine Learning Components and Matching
sections.text: The system determines document relevancy using a word2vec model trained on 10 years of PubMed abstracts [3] [1]. Relevancy is calculated by measuring the distance, defined as 1 minus Cosine Similarity, between the "Health Status Risk Factor" and the document; if this distance is below a specific threshold, the document is deemed relevant [1]. A matching algorithm, originally developed by Schwemmer et al. (2019), is used to assess document relevancy against "gold standard graphs" that were manually annotated from approximately 2,000 clinical quality measure (CQM) descriptions [1]. While this matching process relies on manually annotated knowledge from domain-specific documentations [1], the OATS system is designed to apply this framework to gap areas where evidential support exists but domain documentation is lacking [1].

sections.text: The system demonstrates high precision across various risk factors. For hypertension, precision is 0.93 and recall is 0.84 [1]. For diabetes, precision is 0.92 and recall is 0.76 [1]. sections.title: Broader Context and Future Directions
sections.text: Semantics-based document analysis has significantly improved the performance of document summarization systems [7]. The UNseL method focuses on extracting ontological representations. While simultaneous reading and writing remains challenging [5], dynamic or adaptive ontology summarization is viewed as an interesting topic for future exploration [4]. Defining new measures, whether graph-based or not, is also recommended as a research activity in the context of ontology summarization [4]. question: How can question generation be used to mitigate hallucination in LLMs?

sections.title: The Generation Risk and Retrieval Solutions
sections.text: The core issue is that the generation step of Large Language Models (LLMs) introduces the risk of hallucination, where models create plausible but factually incorrect answers [1]. To address this, a retrieval mechanism that precisely identifies relevant text and removes the generation step is considered a practical and useful approach [1]. Specifically, a novel question-to-question (Q2Q) retrieval approach for open-domain question answering over Wikipedia and Wikidata achieves high precision and eliminates the risk of hallucination by avoiding the generation step [1]. This method argues that precisely identifying relevant text to remove the generation step is a promising strategy for mitigating hallucination in Wikipedia QA [1]. However, conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models suffer from a significant limitation: low semantic similarity between vector embeddings of natural language questions and typical document passages [1]. To overcome this, the Q2Q method employs an instruction-tuned LLM to generate a comprehensive set of questions for each logical content unit within the knowledge base, rather than embedding document content directly [1]. For Wikidata, where content consists of entity relations, the system generates all possible questions to make the knowledge graph accessible to a question-answering system [1].

sections.title: Question Generation Frameworks and Metrics
sections.text: Beyond retrieval, specific frameworks utilize question generation to manage hallucinations. The CQ²A framework extracts entities and relationships from the context to serve as answers, subsequently generating corresponding questions in an answer-first approach [4]. This study leverages the strong text generation capabilities of LLMs to generate questions given a specific context and answer [4]. In the domain of multi-hop questions, the DPKG framework excels at local matching and capturing long-range semantic dependencies, as reflected in its higher BLEU-4 and ROUGE-L scores [3]. Notably, DPKG outperforms the representative model CQG, which relies on question keywords during the generation process, highlighting the positive impact of dual-perspective keywords in guiding multi-hop question generation [3]. However, eliminating hallucinations when prompting LLMs to generate multi-hop questions remains an interesting challenge [3]. To reduce hallucinations in the analysis phase, one method divides the question analysis into two parts executed within a single LLM call using an example-based prompt [2]. A second step involves generating an LLM indicator that encapsulates all topic entities and predicts the answer [2]. Additionally, decomposing complex questions into simpler questions based on identified topic entities guides the LLM to better answer, thereby reducing hallucinations [2].

sections.text: Hallucinations in generated questions may introduce information not present in the source context or violate the constraints specified in the prompt [4]. To test the frequency of these hallucinations, a novel framework generates invalid questions, motivated by findings that language models are overfitting to QA datasets [6]. A self-reflection approach has been shown to result in zero invalid generations at test time. For broader mitigation, using Reinforcement Learning with AI feedback combined with hallucination detection modules may be a potential solution [7]. A comprehensive survey by Ji et al. (2023) summarizes metrics and hallucination detection and mitigation methods for abstractive summarization, dialogue generation, generative question-answering, data-to-text generation, and machine translation [6]. Ultimately, mitigating hallucinations is essential for the safe and responsible deployment of LLMs [5].

question: How can the integration of GIS spatial analysis techniques with economic modeling improve the accuracy and effectiveness of environmental policy ?

sections.title: Spatial Statistical Integration
sections.text: The combination of spatial statistical analysis with Geographic Information Systems (GIS) offers a more sophisticated framework for regional economic analysis [1]. This integration allows researchers to effectively manage changes in the level of the research area, such as shifting from small geographical units to larger ones [1]. Furthermore, the system is convenient for capturing the effect of a larger region on one of its specific components [1]. By facilitating these multi-scale analyses, GIS technology provides a robust foundation for enhancing the precision of economic assessments within environmental contexts.

sections.title: Coupling Environmental and Economic Models
sections.text: Environmental modeling activities can tremendously benefit from the application of GIS technology [3]. The integration of environmental models with GIS functionalities is conceivable through either a loosely or tightly coupled approach [3]. A specific example of this integration involves a study that combines an economic model of climate change with a small structural model of the Greenland ice sheet [2]. This methodology provides a framework for incorporating large earth system changes into standard economic cost-benefit or damage-limiting analyses [2]. However, the study finds that adding the Greenland ice sheet has only a small effect on the social cost of carbon (SCC) because melting is slow and damages are far in the future [2].

sections.title: System Dynamics and Spatial Challenges
sections.text: System dynamics (SD) theory has long been deployed in modeling complex non-linear interrelationships [4]. Despite its utility, it has not been common to use SD modeling in support of bringing environmental sustainability policies to practice [4]. This limitation is largely because the challenge of including spatial data in SD modeling has not yet been well met [4]. Consequently, the potential for the adoption of SD and GIS methods in combination remains a significant area for development, as exemplified in recent studies [4]. Addressing the gap in spatial data integration is crucial for leveraging SD theory in practical environmental policy applications.

sections.text: Effective implementation of these complex models requires specific pedagogical and computational strategies. The just-in-time principle suggests that, instead of teaching software interfaces and features, problems are selected to solve, and only a limited set of tools is taught; those pieces which are necessary to solve the problem are prioritized [5]. Additionally, the concept of autonomation, defined as automation with a human touch, is supported by the functional programming approach of Sprego [5]. This approach requires human intervention to ensure that automated processes align with the nuanced requirements of environmental and economic modeling.
